claim: Motor and non-motor crosslinking proteins play critical roles in determining the size and stability of microtubule-based architectures.
source: Motor and non-motor crosslinking proteins play critical roles in determining the size and stability of microtubule-based architectures.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by citations in the introduction section (Dogterom and Surrey, 2013; Subramanian and Kapoor, 2012; Bratman and Chang, 2008).

claim: The collective activity of PRC1 and Kif4A results in their accumulation at microtubule plus-ends ('end-tag').
source: The collective activity of PRC1 and Kif4A also results in their accumulation at microtubule plus-ends ('end-tag').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1B-E and described in the Results section.

claim: Sliding stalls when the end-tags on antiparallel microtubules collide, forming a stable overlap.
source: Sliding stalls when the end-tags on antiparallel microtubules collide, forming a stable overlap.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figures 1B-D, F-H and described in the Results section.

claim: Sliding velocity scales with initial microtubule-overlap length.
source: First, sliding velocity scales with initial microtubule-overlap length.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4A-B and described in the Results section.

claim: The width of the final overlap scales with microtubule lengths.
source: Second, the width of the final overlap scales with microtubule lengths.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-E and described in the Results section.

claim: PRC1 is an evolutionarily conserved non-motor antiparallel microtubule crosslinking protein.
source: These evolutionarily conserved proteins play an important role in organizing microtubule arrays in interphase yeast and plant cells, and subsets of spindle microtubules in dividing cells in all eukaryotes (Chan et al., 1999; Loïodice et al., 2005; Yamashita et al., 2005; Jiang et al., 1998; Mollinari et al., 2002; Polak et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The velocity of Kif4A motor movement is reduced at end-tags.
source: (i) the velocity of the motor movement is reduced at end-tags (Subramanian et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The size of end-tags increases with microtubule length.
source: (ii) The size of end-tags increases with microtubule length (Subramanian et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Time-lapse imaging shows an enhanced accumulation of Kif4A-GFP at the plus-ends of both the crosslinked microtubules.
source: In addition, time-lapse imaging shows an enhanced accumulation of Kif4A-GFP at the plus-ends of both the crosslinked microtubules.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1B-E.

claim: Under experimental conditions with 0.2 nM PRC1 and 6 nM Kif4A-GFP, Kif4A-GFP-containing end-tags are established at the plus-ends of crosslinked microtubules.
source: Therefore, under these experimental conditions Kif4A-GFP-containing end-tags are established at the plus-ends of crosslinked microtubules.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: End-tagged antiparallel microtubules slide relative to each other.
source: Time-lapse imaging and kymography-based analyses revealed that the end-tagged antiparallel microtubules slide relative to each other (Figure 1B–D and F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1B-D and F-H.

claim: Microtubule sliding stalls when the end-tags arrive at close proximity.
source: Strikingly, we find that microtubule sliding stalls when the end-tags arrive at close proximity (Figure 1B–D and F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1B-D and F-H.

claim: Sliding and stalling of antiparallel microtubules by PRC1 and Kif4A result in the assembly of a stable overlap that is spatially restricted to the filament plus-ends.
source: Consequently, sliding and stalling of antiparallel microtubules by PRC1 and Kif4A result in the assembly of a stable overlap that is spatially restricted to the filament plus-ends.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations shown in Figure 1B-D and F-H.

claim: Under experimental conditions with 0.2 nM PRC1 and 6 nM Kif4A-GFP, the moving microtubule does not slide past the end-tag of the immobilized microtubule.
source: Under these experimental conditions, we do not observe any event where the moving microtubule slides past the end-tag of the immobilized microtubule.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The formation of stable antiparallel overlaps is due to the end-tags on the crosslinked microtubule pair arriving at close proximity during relative sliding.
source: These observations indicate that the formation of stable antiparallel overlaps is due to the end-tags on the crosslinked microtubule pair arriving at close proximity during relative sliding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: The localization pattern of GFP-PRC1 is similar to Kif4A with the highest fluorescence intensity at the end-tags, intermediate intensity at the untagged microtubule overlap regions and the lowest intensity on single microtubules.
source: We find that the localization pattern of GFP-PRC1 is similar to Kif4A with the highest fluorescence intensity at the end-tags, intermediate intensity at the untagged microtubule overlap regions and the lowest intensity on single microtubules.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1I-K.

claim: Human PRC1-Kif4A complexes can drive the relative sliding of antiparallel microtubules over the distance of several microns.
source: Together, these observations suggest that human PRC1-Kif4A complexes can drive the relative sliding of antiparallel microtubules over the distance of several microns.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations shown in Figures 1F-K.

claim: Sliding comes to a halt at microtubule plus-ends resulting in the formation of stable antiparallel overlaps of constant steady-state length.
source: However, sliding comes to a halt at microtubule plus-ends resulting in the formation of stable antiparallel overlaps of constant steady-state length.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations shown in Figures 1F-K.

claim: Dose-dependent microtubule binding of the C-terminus PRC1 and DNA-binding domain of Kif4A (aa. 733–1232) was not observed in the tubulin concentration range tested.
source: Dose-dependent microtubule binding of this domain was not observed in the tubulin concentration range tested.
evidence: This claim is supported by the microtubule co-sedimentation assay shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In the cross-bridging complex, the C-terminus of Kif4A is likely to associate with the N-terminus of PRC1, which forms the link between both microtubules.
source: Therefore, in the cross-bridging complex, the C-terminus of Kif4A is likely to associate with the N-terminus of PRC1, which forms the link between both microtubules (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the microtubule co-sedimentation assay results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Full-length human Kif4A does not bundle microtubules in the presence of ATP.
source: Similar to a previous report with Xklp1, full-length human Kif4A does not bundle microtubules in the presence of ATP (not shown) (Bieling et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and a citation to prior work.

claim: The predominant angle of initial attachment between two microtubules crosslinked by Kif4A alone is 0–30°.
source: We find that the predominant angle of initial attachment between the two microtubules is 0–30° (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Contact between the end-tag on the non-biotinylated microtubule with the immobilized microtubule results in tip-mediated movement of one microtubule over the other.
source: We find that contact between the end-tag on the non-biotinylated microtubule with the immobilized microtubule results in tip-mediated movement of one microtubule over the other (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Similar to experiments with PRC1 and Kif4A, sliding completely stalls when the Kif4A-GFP end-tags collide in experiments with Kif4A alone.
source: Similar to experiments with PRC1 and Kif4A, sliding completely stalls when the Kif4A-GFP end-tags collide.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: A Kif4A-dense microtubule tip can slide along another microtubule even though the C-terminus of Kif4A does not bind microtubules with high affinity.
source: These findings indicate that a Kif4A-dense microtubule tip can slide along another microtubule even though the C-terminus of Kif4A does not bind microtubules with high affinity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations shown in Figure 2.

claim: There are two possible modes of cross-bridging and sliding in the PRC1-Kif4A system.
source: Together these findings suggest that there are two possible modes of cross-bridging and sliding in the PRC1-Kif4A system.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations shown in Figure 2.

claim: Kif4A-molecules interacting with microtubule-crosslinking PRC1-molecules can drive sliding.
source: First, Kif4A-molecules interacting with microtubule-crosslinking PRC1-molecules can drive sliding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Kif4A molecules at the tips of one microtubule can bind and slide over another microtubule.
source: Second, Kif4A molecules at the tips of one microtubule can bind and slide over another microtubule.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Relative microtubule movement can stall at microtubule ends in the absence of PRC1.
source: Finally, these experiments show that relative microtubule movement can stall at microtubule ends in the absence of PRC1, suggesting that molecular crowding is likely to be the predominant cause of stable overlap formation in the PRC1-Kif4A system.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations shown in Figure 2.

claim: Molecular crowding is likely to be the predominant cause of stable overlap formation in the PRC1-Kif4A system.
source: Finally, these experiments show that relative microtubule movement can stall at microtubule ends in the absence of PRC1, suggesting that molecular crowding is likely to be the predominant cause of stable overlap formation in the PRC1-Kif4A system.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations shown in Figure 2.

claim: Analysis of the instantaneous velocity during microtubule sliding reveals three phases: (1) initial sliding at constant velocity, (2) reduction in sliding velocity as the end-tags arrive at close proximity, and (3) microtubule stalling and the formation of stable overlaps that persist for the duration of the experiment.
source: Analysis of the instantaneous velocity during microtubule sliding (Figure 3A–C; 0.2 nM PRC1 + 6 nM Kif4A-GFP), reveals three phases: (1) initial sliding at constant velocity, (2) reduction in sliding velocity as the end-tags arrive at close proximity, and (3) microtubule stalling and the formation of stable overlaps that persist for the duration of the experiment.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Increasing the PRC1 solution concentration 5-fold (0.2 and 1 nM) at constant Kif4A-GFP concentration (6 nM) resulted in a 4-fold reduction in the microtubule sliding velocity.
source: We found that increasing the PRC1 solution concentration 5-fold (0.2 and 1 nM) at constant Kif4A-GFP concentration (6 nM) resulted in a 4-fold reduction in the microtubule sliding velocity (velocity = 46 ± 17 nm/s at 0.2 nM and velocity = 11 ± 8 nm/s at 1 nM).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Increasing PRC1 concentration 2-fold (0.5 and 1 nM) at constant Kif4A levels (6 nM) resulted in a ~2 fold reduction in the microtubule sliding velocity.
source: Similarly, in assays with GFP-PRC1 and unlabeled Kif4A, we found that increasing PRC1 concentration 2-fold (0.5 and 1 nM) at constant Kif4A levels (6 nM) resulted in a ~2 fold reduction in the microtubule sliding velocity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; velocity = 30 ± 13 nm/s at 0.5 nM and velocity = 19 ± 8 nm/s at 1 nM PRC1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A 5-fold increase in the PRC1 concentrations results in a 2-fold increase in the average Kif4A density in the untagged overlap region.
source: The data show that a 5-fold increase in the PRC1 concentrations results in a 2-fold increase in the average Kif4A density in the untagged overlap region, indicating that Kif4A is effectively recruited to antiparallel overlaps at the highest PRC1 concentrations in our assays (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The solution concentration ratios of PRC1:Kif4A sets the sliding velocity by determining the relative ratio of sliding-competent PRC1-Kif4A complexes to sliding-inhibiting PRC1 molecules in the antiparallel overlap.
source: Together, these results are consistent with a mechanism in which the solution concentration ratios of PRC1:Kif4A sets the sliding velocity by determining the relative ratio of sliding-competent PRC1-Kif4A complexes to sliding-inhibiting PRC1 molecules in the antiparallel overlap.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations shown in Figures 3D-E.

claim: Antiparallel microtubules with longer initial overlaps slide at a higher velocity than microtubules with shorter initial overlaps under the same experimental condition.
source: Remarkably, analysis of three different datasets suggests that antiparallel microtubules with longer initial overlaps slide at a higher velocity than microtubules with shorter initial overlaps under the same experimental condition (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: No significant correlation was observed between the sum of end-tag lengths or sum of end-tag intensities and sliding velocity.
source: However, no significant correlation was observed between the sum of end-tag lengths or sum of end-tag intensities and sliding velocity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: The average sliding velocity (75 ± 25 nm/s; N = 25) is independent of end-tag intensity in experiments with Kif4A alone.
source: Consistent with this, the average sliding velocity (75 ± 25 nm/s; N = 25) is independent of end-tag intensity in experiments with Kif4A alone (Figure 2C–D) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1Q).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1Q.

claim: The sliding velocity increases with the initial untagged overlap length under all the conditions where length-dependent sliding is observed.
source: Instead, we find that in experiments with PRC1 and Kif4A, the sliding velocity increases with the initial untagged overlap length under all the conditions where length-dependent sliding is observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: Kif4A-GFP intensity is proportional to both the total and untagged overlap lengths.
source: Under these conditions, Kif4A-GFP intensity is proportional to both the total and untagged overlap lengths, suggesting that sliding velocity scales with the number of molecules in the overlap (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D inset; Note: intensity is a measure of the total number of molecules in the overlap, it is not a direct measure of the number of Kif4A motors involved in binding PRC1 and sliding. We assume that the number of sliding-competent motors is proportional to total intensity).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: No correlation is found between sliding velocity and the average motor density in the untagged overlap during phase-1 movement.
source: In addition, no correlation is found between sliding velocity and the average motor density in the untagged overlap during phase-1 movement (0.2 nM PRC1 and 6 nM Kif4A-GFP; Pearson's coefficient: −0.15; N = 20) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Sliding velocity is set by the total number of sliding-competent PRC1-Kif4A molecules in the untagged region of the antiparallel microtubule overlap.
source: These data are consistent with a mechanism in which sliding velocity is set by the total number of sliding-competent PRC1-Kif4A molecules in the untagged region of the antiparallel microtubule overlap.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Longer microtubules typically form longer initial overlaps that exhibit faster sliding.
source: A scatter plot of the sliding velocity as a function of initial overlap length color-coded by the moving-microtubule length shows that longer microtubules typically form longer initial overlaps that exhibit faster sliding (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: The dominant contribution to the sliding velocity is from the initial overlap length.
source: However, the observation that long microtubules that form short overlaps exhibit slower sliding than long microtubules that form long overlaps (for example: 6 μm microtubules with ~3 μm overlap in Figure 4C, blue dots), suggests the dominant contribution to the sliding velocity is from the initial overlap length (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: The initial length of the antiparallel overlap can tune the microtubule sliding velocity, such that longer overlaps, which have a greater number of PRC1-Kif4A molecules, slide at a faster rate than shorter microtubule overlaps.
source: Our findings indicate that the initial length of the antiparallel overlap can tune the microtubule sliding velocity, such that longer overlaps, which have a greater number of PRC1-Kif4A molecules, slide at a faster rate than shorter microtubule overlaps.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations shown in Figure 4.

claim: In all events where the reduction in overlap length begins from the initial time point of recording, movement velocity is constant during phase-1 as the overlap length continually shrinks during sliding.
source: We find that in all of these events, movement velocity is constant during phase-1 as the overlap length continually shrinks during sliding (Figure 4E–H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–P, 2F-H and N-P).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E-H and Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Sliding velocity scales with initial overlap length under equilibrium conditions.
source: We examined events in which phase-1 sliding continued after the establishment of constant motor number and find that sliding velocity scales with initial overlap length under equilibrium conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The velocity of microtubule sliding in the PRC1-Kif4A system is determined by the initial width of the PRC1-crosslinked antiparallel overlap, which sets the total number of sliding competent molecules in the untagged overlap.
source: These data, together with the observation that the number of molecules in the end-tag does not contribute significantly to sliding velocity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1Q and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B), indicate that the velocity of microtubule sliding in the PRC1-Kif4A system is determined by the initial width of the PRC1-crosslinked antiparallel overlap, which sets the total number of sliding competent molecules in the untagged overlap.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: During microtubule sliding at phase-1, the increase in the density of motor molecules could compensate for the reduction in overlap length and the number of sliding-competent motors, ensuring that microtubule-movement proceeds at a constant velocity.
source: During microtubule sliding at phase-1, the increase in the density of motor molecules could compensate for the reduction in overlap length and the number of sliding-competent motors, ensuring that microtubule-movement proceeds at a constant velocity.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: The transition from phase-1 to phase-2 does not coincide with a shift from constant to decreasing overlap length during sliding.
source: As discussed in the previous section, our results show that the transition from phase-1 to phase-2 does not coincide with a shift from constant to decreasing overlap length during sliding, and there is no inverse correlation between Kif4A-GFP density and the sliding velocity during phase-1 movement under the same experimental condition (See Figure 4E–H, Figure 4—figure supplements 1G–P and and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E-H and Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: In 50% of the events (47/98; 0.2 nM PRC1 + 6 nM Kif4A-GFP), the transition from phase 1 to 2 occurs when the end-tags have nearly merged.
source: We noticed that in 50% of the events (47/98; 0.2 nM PRC1 + 6 nM Kif4A-GFP), the transition from phase 1 to 2 occurs when the end-tags have nearly merged and our image analysis algorithm does not resolve the two end-tags (examples in Figure 4E–H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–P).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E-H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G-P.

claim: Kif4A-GFP density measurement and fluorescence line-scan analysis at the phase-1 to phase-2 transition time-points in two experimental conditions show that the protein density at the phase-1 to phase-2 transition is similar under different experimental conditions.
source: Kif4A-GFP density measurement and fluorescence line-scan analysis at the phase-1 to phase-2 transition time-points in two experimental conditions show that this is indeed the case (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A-B.

claim: On average slowdown occurs when the intensity is >70% of the average end-tag intensity.
source: Furthermore, comparison of the phase-1 to phase-2 transition-point intensity with the average end-tag intensity suggests that on average slowdown occurs when the intensity is >70% of the average end-tag intensity (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B-C.

claim: Sliding slows down proximal to end-tags, when the untagged overlap is short and the motors encounter a high-density region, where stepping is inhibited.
source: These observations suggest that sliding slows down proximal to end-tags, when the untagged overlap is short and the motors encounter a high-density region, where stepping is inhibited.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The width of the stable microtubule overlap established by PRC1 and Kif4A is approximately equal to the sum of the end-tag lengths on both microtubules.
source: These findings indicate that the width of the stable microtubule overlap established by PRC1 and Kif4A is approximately equal to the sum of the end-tag lengths on both microtubules.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Under the lowest PRC1 concentration tested, the end-tagged regions of the microtubules have a greater fraction of unoccupied sites that allows for further sliding and reduction in the overlap length after the collision of end-tags.
source: A possible reason is that under these conditions, the end-tagged regions of the microtubules have a greater fraction of unoccupied sites that allows for further sliding and reduction in the overlap length after the collision of end-tags.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observation in Figure 5B.

claim: The final overlap length increases linearly with microtubule length.
source: In all three cases, we find that the final overlap length increases linearly with microtubule length (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: The slope of the line relating final overlap length to microtubule length is higher at greater PRC1 concentration due to longer end-tags formed under these conditions.
source: The slope of the line is higher at greater PRC1 concentration due to longer end-tags formed under these conditions (Figure 5E; 0.2 nM PRC1 + 6 nM Kif4A-GFP, slope = 0.3; 1 nM PRC1 + 6 nM Kif4A-GFP, slope = 0.8).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: PRC1-Kif4A end-tags act as a barrier to microtubule sliding and establish a stable antiparallel overlap whose size is determined by the microtubule lengths.
source: These data suggest that PRC1-Kif4A end-tags act as a barrier to microtubule sliding and establish a stable antiparallel overlap whose size is determined by the microtubule lengths.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations shown in Figure 5.

claim: While PRC1 was retained in the region of the microtubule overlap under no-nucleotide conditions, the width of the antiparallel overlap did not change during the course of the experiment.
source: Image analysis revealed that while PRC1 was retained in the region of the microtubule overlap under these conditions, the width of the antiparallel overlap did not change during the course of the experiment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: No overlap expansion was observed when the final buffer was supplemented with 2 mM ADP.
source: As shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–F, no overlap expansion was observed under these conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-F.

claim: The inclusion of 1 nM PRC1 in addition to 2 mM ADP in the final buffer did not promote overlap expansion.
source: The inclusion of 1 nM PRC1 in addition to 2 mM ADP in the final buffer also did not promote overlap expansion (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G-H.

claim: Neither motor deactivation with ADP nor increasing the number of PRC1 molecules is sufficient to induce entropic expansions of measurable magnitude in the PRC1-Kif4A system.
source: Therefore, neither motor deactivation with ADP nor increasing the number of PRC1 molecules is sufficient to induce entropic expansions of measurable magnitude in this system, suggesting that an alternative mechanism is likely responsible for countering the Kif4A-mediated sliding forces in the antiparallel overlap.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Re-introducing ATP after ADP exchange allows motor-protein stepping and reinitiates microtubule sliding.
source: To test this experimentally, we introduced buffer containing 1 mM ATP (no additional protein) into the chamber 15 min after the ADP exchange step (Figure 6D). We find that relative microtubule sliding is reinitiated under these conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: New end-tags are established during microtubule sliding after ATP re-introduction, which subsequently collide to establish a new stable antiparallel overlap of shorter width.
source: Analysis of the GFP fluorescence-intensity profile at different time-points post buffer exchange revealed that new end-tags are established during microtubule sliding, which subsequently collide to establish a new stable antiparallel overlap of shorter width (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: PRC1-Kif4A end-tags establish stable overlaps by sterically hindering the relative sliding of antiparallel microtubules.
source: Together, these findings are consistent with a mechanism in which PRC1-Kif4A end-tags establish stable overlaps by sterically hindering the relative sliding of antiparallel microtubules.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations shown in Figure 6.

claim: A 'molecular road-block' based mechanism provides a simple explanation for the observed correlation between the sum of end-tag lengths and the final overlap length in the PRC1-Kif4A system.
source: Such a 'molecular road-block' based mechanism also provides a simple explanation for the observed correlation between the sum of end-tag lengths and the final overlap length in this system.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Both sliding microtubules stall proximal to the plus end-tag on the immobilized microtubule in events where two microtubules slide relative to a single immobilized microtubule.
source: In these events (Figure 7A–C; 0.2 nM PRC1 + 6 nM Kif4A-GFP), we observed that both the sliding microtubules stall proximal to the plus end-tag on the immobilized microtubule.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: The formation of end-tags on single microtubules can establish an antiparallel array composed of multiple microtubules with closely aligned plus-ends.
source: The data suggest that the formation of end-tags on single microtubules can establish an antiparallel array composed of multiple microtubules with closely aligned plus-ends.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations shown in Figure 7.

claim: Microtubule sliding and stalling by PRC1 and Kif4A can align multiple antiparallel filaments such that the region of overlap is restricted to the plus-ends of all the microtubules.
source: Together, these observations suggest that microtubule sliding and stalling by PRC1 and Kif4A can align multiple antiparallel filaments such that the region of overlap is restricted to the plus-ends of all the microtubules.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations shown in Figure 7.

claim: PRC1 specifically crosslinks and preferentially localizes to the region of overlap between two antiparallel microtubules.
source: PRC1 specifically crosslinks and preferentially localizes to the region of overlap between two antiparallel microtubules (Figure 8A) (Bieling et al., 2010; Subramanian et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and experimental observations in this study.

claim: Kif4A is recruited to the antiparallel overlap through direct interaction with PRC1.
source: Kif4A is recruited to the antiparallel overlap through direct interaction with PRC1 (Bieling et al., 2010; Subramanian et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The highly processive movement of PRC1-Kif4A complexes on microtubules and the slow dissociation of these proteins from microtubule plus-ends result in the formation of 'end-tags'.
source: The highly processive movement of PRC1-Kif4A complexes on microtubules and the slow dissociation of these proteins from microtubule plus-ends result in the formation of 'end-tags', which are highly crowded regions in which motor stepping is inhibited (Figure 8A) (Subramanian et al., 2013; Leduc et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and experimental observations in this study.

claim: The activity of PRC1-Kif4A complexes within antiparallel overlaps results in robust relative microtubule sliding.
source: In addition, the activity of PRC1-Kif4A complexes within antiparallel overlaps results in robust relative microtubule sliding (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Microtubule movement first slows down and then stalls when the two end-tags arrive at close proximity during relative sliding, resulting in the formation of a stable antiparallel overlap.
source: Microtubule movement first slows down and then stalls when the two end-tags arrive at close proximity during relative sliding, resulting in the formation of a stable antiparallel overlap (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Steric hindrance is likely to be the predominant cause of stable overlap formation in the PRC1-Kif4A system.
source: In contrast, we propose that the predominant mechanism that leads to the formation of a stable overlap in the PRC1-Kif4A system is steric hindrance to motor stepping at regions of high protein-density for the following reasons.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on multiple lines of evidence from the experimental observations.

claim: Sliding microtubules come to a stall when the PRC1-Kif4A end-tags arrive at close proximity.
source: First, sliding microtubules come to a stall when the PRC1-Kif4A end-tags arrive at close proximity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: The PRC1 and Kif4A binding sites at the end-tag region of the microtubule are likely to be nearly saturated.
source: Steric hindrance at an end-tag is expected to be high because the PRC1 and Kif4A binding sites at this region of the microtubule are likely to be nearly saturated (Subramanian et al., 2013; Leduc et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on citations to prior work.

claim: The accumulation of Kif4A alone at microtubule ends can stop sliding.
source: Second, the accumulation of Kif4A alone at microtubule ends can stop sliding, and full-length Kif4A does not have a C-terminus non-motor domain that binds tightly to microtubules and is therefore unlikely to generate significant frictional forces (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Entropic force driven expansion of stable overlaps formed by PRC1 and Kif4A is not observed when the motor is deactivated.
source: Third, we do not observe entropic force driven expansion of stable overlaps formed by PRC1 and Kif4A when the motor is deactivated (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 6.

claim: There is no inverse correlation between sliding velocity and changes in protein density during phase-1 sliding.
source: Fourth, we do not observe an inverse correlation between sliding velocity and changes in protein density during phase-1 sliding as is predicted in models where the buildup of opposing forces in shrinking overlaps stall microtubule sliding (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The frictional forces generated by PRC1 are low.
source: Finally, previous studies have shown that the frictional forces generated by PRC1 are low, and the speed of Kif4A movement on single microtubules is not affected by PRC1 (Duellberg et al., 2013; Forth et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The speed of Kif4A movement on single microtubules is not affected by PRC1.
source: Finally, previous studies have shown that the frictional forces generated by PRC1 are low, and the speed of Kif4A movement on single microtubules is not affected by PRC1 (Duellberg et al., 2013; Forth et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The number of PRC1 molecules is less than Kif4A motors at the microtubule overlap in the experiments.
source: Combined with the observation that the number of PRC1 molecules is less than Kif4A motors at the microtubule overlap in our experiments (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), it is unlikely that stable overlaps can be formed solely through the opposition of Kif4A-generated forces by PRC1 at end-tags.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Steric hindrance is likely to play an important role in switching from sliding at constant velocity to slowdown at the phase-1 to phase-2 transition.
source: For similar reasons as stated above, steric hindrance is likely to play an important role in switching from sliding at constant velocity to slowdown at the phase-1 to phase-2 transition (Figures 3C and 4F), and the reduction in average sliding velocity at high PRC1 concentrations (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: The PRC1-Kif4A system reveals an alternative mechanism in which a motor and a non-motor protein act synergistically on antiparallel microtubules to first promote relative sliding and then stall microtubule movement by forming a molecular roadblock.
source: Overall, in contrast to mechanisms where stable microtubule arrays are organized through opposing forces generated by a pair of motor and non-motor protein, the PRC1-Kif4A system reveals an alternative mechanism in which a motor and a non-motor protein act synergistically on antiparallel microtubules to first promote relative sliding and then stall microtubule movement by forming a molecular roadblock.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and comparison with other systems.

claim: In the PRC1-Kif4A system, stable arrays can be established under conditions where the non-motor:motor protein ratio may not be sufficiently high to achieve force-balance.
source: First, in this system, stable arrays can be established under conditions where the non-motor:motor protein ratio may not be not sufficiently high to achieve force-balance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proposed roadblock mechanism.

claim: The roadblock mechanism allows for robust relative sliding until the end-tags collide.
source: Second, this system allows for robust relative sliding until the end-tags collide.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: The roadblock mechanism leads to the establishment of stable antiparallel overlaps that are spatially restricted to microtubule plus-ends.
source: This in turn leads to the establishment of stable antiparallel overlaps that are spatially restricted to microtubule plus-ends.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: The roadblock mechanism provides a simple mechanism by which the formation of length-dependent PRC1-Kif4A end-tags on single microtubules can be readily translated to the organization of microtubule overlaps whose size scales with microtubule length.
source: Third, it provides a simple mechanism by which the formation of length-dependent PRC1-Kif4A end-tags on single microtubules can be readily translated to the organization of microtubule overlaps whose size scales with microtubule length (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Kif4A alone does not promote antiparallel microtubule crosslinking.
source: We find that (i) Kif4A alone does not promote antiparallel microtubule crosslinking and (ii) the C-terminus tail of Kif4A does not interact with microtubules with binding affinities comparable to other microtubule binding domains (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There is no evidence for significant oligomerization of full-length Kif4A in the micromolar concentration range.
source: In addition, currently there is no evidence for significant oligomerization of full-length Kif4A in the micromolar concentration range (~10 μM).
evidence: This is a statement about the lack of evidence for oligomerization.

claim: A fraction of Kif4A molecules at the very tip of the microtubule may adopt a one-head bound state and collectively mediate microtubule sliding.
source: We speculate that since end-tags are highly crowded regions, a fraction of Kif4A molecules, especially those at the very tip of the microtubule, may adopt a one-head bound state (as is seen in EM experiments performed at high concentrations of kinesin dimers (Hoenger et al., 2000; Hirose et al., 2000), and collectively mediate microtubule sliding.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism based on prior EM observations.

claim: The C-terminus of Kif4A is likely to interact with the N-terminus of PRC1 in the untagged overlaps.
source: Instead, the C-terminus of Kif4A is likely to interact with the N-terminus of PRC1 (Kd = 0.3 μM) (Subramanian et al., 2013), and the PRC1-tethered Kif4A complexes within the untagged region of the antiparallel overlap drive sliding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured dissociation constant and experimental observations.

claim: PRC1 and Kif4A are unlikely to form a stable long-lived complex.
source: However, PRC1 and Kif4A are unlikely to form a stable long-lived complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the inability to isolate stable complexes.

claim: PRC1-Kif4A complexes have a longer microtubule lifetime than either protein alone.
source: However, PRC1-Kif4A complexes have a longer microtubule lifetime than either protein alone, suggesting that PRC1 and Kif4A molecules likely undergo dynamic dissociation and re-association on microtubules (Bieling et al., 2010; Subramanian et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The scaling of movement velocity with motor number has been proposed for microtubule-based transport of cargoes in the cellular cytoplasm.
source: While the scaling of movement velocity with motor number has been proposed for microtubule-based transport of cargoes in the cellular cytoplasm (Hill et al., 2004; Kural et al., 2005; Levi et al., 2006), it is not typically observed in microtubule sliding by an ensemble of processive kinesins in in vitro assays.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Scaling of sliding velocity with microtubule overlap length can be observed in the absence of substantial external viscous drag forces.
source: However, this study and in vitro reconstitution experiments with mixtures of Ncd and Ase1 or with the kinesin-14 HSET alone show that scaling of sliding velocity with microtubule overlap length can be observed in the absence of substantial external viscous drag forces (Braun et al., 2017; Braun et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations in this study and citations to prior work.

claim: In both the Ncd-Ase1 and HSET systems, reduction in sliding velocity within shrinking overlap occurs concurrently with an increase in protein density.
source: However, the mechanisms by which length-dependent sliding is achieved in these systems differ. In both the Ncd-Ase1 and HSET systems, reduction in sliding velocity within shrinking overlap occurs concurrently with an increase in protein density (Braun et al., 2017; Braun et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the PRC1-Kif4A system, the initial velocity is constant and does not change with reducing overlap length or changes in motor density during sliding.
source: However, in the PRC1-Kif4A system, the initial velocity is constant and does not change with reducing overlap length or changes in motor density during sliding (examples in Figure 4E–H, Figure 4—figure supplements 1G–P and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E-H and Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: In the constant velocity phase of the PRC1-Kif4A system, the rate of microtubule movement is determined by the initial overlap width, which determines the number of associated motor molecules.
source: In this constant velocity phase, the rate of microtubule movement is determined by the initial overlap width, which determines the number of associated motor molecules.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: The mechanism of overlap length-dependent sliding by PRC1 and Kif4A is different from systems that involve an increase in forces that oppose motor movement in shrinking overlaps during microtubule sliding.
source: Therefore, the mechanism of overlap length-dependent sliding by PRC1 and Kif4A is different from systems that involve an increase in forces that oppose motor movement in shrinking overlaps during microtubule sliding.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with other systems.

claim: When kinesin motors are anchored to a diffusive lipid surface instead of a rigid glass coverslip, the gliding velocity of attached microtubules is dependent on the number of motor molecules.
source: For example, when kinesin motors are anchored to a diffusive lipid surface instead of a rigid glass coverslip, the gliding velocity of attached microtubules is dependent on the number of motor molecules (Grover et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The measured dissociation constant between the C-terminus of Kif4A and the N-terminus of PRC1 is 0.3 μM.
source: The measured dissociation constant between the C-terminus of Kif4A and the N-terminus of PRC1 is 0.3 μM, suggesting that these proteins do not form a stable long-lived complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Subramanian et al., 2013).

claim: The 'moving' microtubule is likely to be loosely coupled to the kinesin walking on an immobilized microtubule.
source: Therefore the 'moving' microtubule is likely to be loosely coupled to the kinesin walking on an immobilized microtubule, and each 8 nm step of the kinesin does not translate into an 8 nm displacement of the moving microtubule.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured dissociation constant.

claim: Force-dependent dissociation of PRC1-microtubule interaction during kinesin stepping will further reduce the coupling between the two microtubules.
source: Other factors, such as force-dependent dissociation of PRC1-microtubule interaction during kinesin stepping, will further reduce the coupling between the two microtubules, and result in the reduction in the 'sliding efficiency', and consequently, the sliding velocity in the PRC1-Kif4A system.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about factors affecting sliding efficiency.

claim: Microtubule sliding by the PRC1-Kif4A complex can be considered as microtubule movement driven by an ensemble of low sliding efficiency motors.
source: Together, our findings suggest that microtubule sliding by the PRC1-Kif4A complex can be considered as microtubule movement driven by an ensemble of low sliding efficiency motors, which results in the scaling of microtubule sliding velocity with antiparallel overlap length.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and calculations.

claim: A defining architectural feature of the spindle midzone is a stable antiparallel microtubule array with overlapping plus-ends.
source: A defining architectural feature of the spindle midzone is a stable antiparallel microtubule array with overlapping plus-ends (Bratman and Chang, 2008; Glotzer, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The relative sliding of PRC1-crosslinked microtubules by motor proteins is thought to mediate the spindle elongation during early anaphase and contribute to defining the overlap width.
source: The relative sliding of PRC1-crosslinked microtubules by motor proteins such as Cin8 and Kip3p in budding yeast and KLP61F in Drosophila is thought to mediate the spindle elongation during early anaphase and contribute to defining the overlap width (Sharp et al., 1999; Straight et al., 1998; Pellman et al., 1995; Su et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Antiparallel sliding of PRC1-crosslinked inter-kinetochore bridges is required for proper chromosome segregation.
source: Antiparallel sliding of PRC1-crosslinked inter-kinetochore bridges is required for proper chromosome segregation (Polak et al., 2017; Vukušić et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Initial overlap length-dependent sliding could be advantageous in ensuring that microtubules of different lengths arrive at similar rates to the plus-ends of the template microtubule within arrays.
source: Initial overlap length-dependent sliding could be advantageous in ensuring that microtubules of different lengths arrive at similar rates to the plus-ends of the template microtubule within arrays.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the functional advantage of length-dependent sliding.

claim: The accumulation of proteins at microtubule plus-ends is thought to effectively concentrate cytokinesis factors proximal to the site of cell cleavage.
source: The accumulation of proteins at microtubule plus-ends, including multiple mitotic kinesins, is thought to effectively concentrate cytokinesis factors proximal to the site of cell cleavage (Shrestha et al., 2012; Glotzer, 2009; Canman et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Microtubule-end localization of PRC1 has been reported during monopolar cytokinesis and in bipolar cells.
source: Microtubule-end localization of PRC1 has been reported during monopolar cytokinesis (Subramanian et al., 2013; Shrestha et al., 2012), and in bipolar cells (Shrestha et al., 2012; Shannon et al., 2005), and both PRC1 and Kif4A have been described to co-localize at the ends of astral arrays of Xenopus egg extracts (Nguyen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Dense regions of proteins at microtubule ends may contribute to the alignment and stability of antiparallel microtubule arrays.
source: These dense regions of proteins at microtubule ends may contribute to the alignment and stability of antiparallel microtubule arrays.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: The roadblock mechanism may be utilized by other kinesins that accumulate at microtubule plus-ends for the organization of stable arrays of defined size and geometry.
source: Furthermore, the roadblock mechanism may be utilized by other kinesins that accumulate at microtubule plus-ends for the organization of stable arrays of defined size and geometry (Shimamoto et al., 2015; Braun et al., 2017; Bieling et al., 2010; Braun et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental observations and citations to prior work.

claim: The geometrical features of the microtubules in the spindle can tune the activity of associated proteins and regulate the geometry and stability of cellular microtubule arrays such as the spindle midzone.
source: Our biophysical analyses suggest that the geometrical features of the microtubules in the spindle can in turn tune the activity of associated proteins and regulate the geometry and stability of cellular microtubule arrays such as the spindle midzone.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Filament crosslinking, relative-sliding and molecular crowding are likely to represent general features of a number of biological polymers.
source: Filament crosslinking, relative-sliding and molecular crowding are likely to represent general features of a number of biological polymers, such as actin filaments and nucleic acids, that are dynamically organized during different cellular processes.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the generality of the mechanisms.

claim: The mechanism revealed in this study can represent general principles that regulate the size and dynamics of cellular architectures built from different polymers.
source: The mechanism revealed here can therefore represent general principles that regulate the size and dynamics of cellular architectures built from different polymers.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the generality of the mechanisms.
